opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the honest answer is that there are a few uncertainties, but the one I'd put at the top is whether the optimization problem stays tractable and well-behaved as we scale up.

To back up a bit: the core idea of parameter decomposition is that instead of looking for features in the activations, we decompose the network's weights into a set of components. We want those components to faithfully sum back to the original parameters, we want as few of them as possible to be needed on any given input, and we want each one to be as simple as possible. On toy models, and on small language models, we've gotten that to work reasonably well. Moving from our earlier attribution-based approach to the stochastic version made things much more stable and much less sensitive to hyperparameters, which was a big step.

But when you go to a model with billions of parameters, a few things get harder at once. The first is compute and memory. You're learning a decomposition of every weight matrix, potentially into a very large number of components, and you need enough of them to capture everything the model actually does. So there's a real engineering question about whether we can make that efficient enough to be practical, rather than something that costs many times what it cost to train the model.

The second, and to me the more interesting scientific uncertainty, is whether the decompositions we find at scale will actually be the "right" ones, in the sense of carving the network at its true mechanistic joints. On toy models we often know the ground truth, so we can check. On a large language model we don't. We'll need good ways to tell whether a component reflects a real computational mechanism or is an artifact of the optimization or of the particular way we've set up the loss. Related to that is the question of how much of the model's behavior is captured by relatively clean, sparse mechanisms versus a long tail of messy stuff that resists that kind of description. If the tail is huge, then even a technically successful decomposition might leave a lot unexplained.

And then the third is whether the components will be interpretable to humans at that scale, which is a separate question from whether they're mechanistically faithful. Ideally those line up, but there's no guarantee.

So I'm optimistic. The results on smaller models have been encouraging, and I think parameter decomposition addresses some genuine conceptual problems with activation-based methods, like feature splitting and the difficulty of connecting features to the actual computations performed. But whether it holds up cleanly on frontier-scale models is very much an open empirical question, and that's what a lot of the work now is aimed at answering.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the key uncertainty is whether the thing we're decomposing into actually stays meaningful as you scale. With the toy models and the smaller language models we've worked with, we can look at the components and go, okay, this one is doing this identifiable thing, and we can check that against ground truth, or at least against our intuitions. At scale, you lose that. You don't have ground truth, and the number of components grows enormously, so you're relying on the method itself to tell you that it's found the right decomposition, which is a bit circular.

And there's a more technical version of that worry, which is around the optimization. Parameter decomposition is fundamentally an optimization problem, you're trying to find a set of components whose sum reconstructs the weights, while also satisfying this minimality or simplicity pressure, so that only a few components are needed for any given input. And in small models you can run that optimization to something close to convergence and you can play with the hyperparameters and see what happens. In a model with billions of parameters, the question is, does that loss landscape still have the nice properties we're relying on, or does it become so rugged that you just end up with a local minimum that looks plausible but is actually a mess? I genuinely don't know yet, and I think anyone who claims to know is overclaiming.

The third thing I'd flag is cost. The original formulations were, frankly, very expensive, and a lot of the work we've done since has been about making the method cheap enough to even attempt at scale. We've made real progress there, but there's still an open question about whether the approximations we introduce to make it tractable quietly break the thing that made the method principled in the first place. So it's really those three: does the decomposition remain interpretable, does the optimization remain well-behaved, and can we make it affordable without compromising it. If I had to bet, I'd say the optimization question is the one that keeps me up at night most, because it's the one where a failure might not be obvious. You'd get something that looks fine and isn't.

astra-6.text:
I think the key uncertainty is whether the decomposition will remain both tractable and useful as we scale. Can we break a larger model’s parameters into components that correspond to meaningful pieces of computation, rather than just finding another way to represent the same weights?

Those are different standards. You could get a decomposition that reconstructs the original model very well, but still doesn’t make its behavior much easier to understand. What we’d really like is to identify a component, form a hypothesis about what it does, and then intervene on it and see the predicted effect.

So the question is not just whether we can afford to run the method on a bigger model. It’s whether the resulting components give us enough explanatory and causal leverage to justify doing so.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key uncertainty is whether the decomposition stays useful as you scale. Can we find components that are individually interpretable and that actually explain how the model computes, without needing so many components that we’ve just moved the complexity somewhere else?

There are really two questions there. One is computational: can we make the decomposition cheap enough to run on much larger models? The other is scientific: does the structure we’re looking for emerge cleanly, or do we get components that mix together lots of different behaviors? We could make progress on the engineering and still find that the resulting decomposition isn’t a particularly useful explanation.

So I’d want to test more than whether we can reconstruct the original weights or preserve the model’s performance. Can we use the components to predict what happens when we intervene? Can we explain a behavior we didn’t already understand? That’s the evidence that would make me confident the approach is scaling in the sense we care about.
